 Reporting from Dallas
 Nov. 6, 2026

 Former President George W. Bush and his wife, Laura, are siding with their longtime church and its leaders in the congregation’s high-stakes clash with the United Methodist Church, a spokesman for the couple said this week.
 The Bushes have been members at Highland Park United Methodist Church in Dallas — one of the largest and wealthiest Methodist congregations in the country — since the late 1980s. Last month, the church’s members voted to leave the national denomination, the latest salvo in an intense public battle for control of the congregation’s assets and its identity.
 Mr. and Mrs. Bush participated in the congregation’s recent vote to leave the denomination, Mr. Bush’s chief of staff, Freddy Ford, told The New York Times on Thursday. The vote took place in person at the church in October. Of the 4,775 votes cast, just over 90 percent favored departing the United Methodist Church.
 The Bushes “are grateful to Reverend Matt Tuggle for so faithfully guiding the congregation through these rough waters,” Mr. Ford said, referring to the church’s senior minister.
 The statement is the Bushes’ first public comment on the controversy that is roiling their usually decorous church community — and reverberating far outside Texas.
 What began as a quiet ecclesiastical dispute burst into public view in August, when the United Methodist bishop overseeing Highland Park, Ruben Saenz Jr., sued it over changes to its bylaws . The church has since waged an unusually public campaign pushing back, with the congregation’s leadership board saying that the denomination had “irrevocably broken the bond of trust that once existed between our Church and The United Methodist Church.”
